entries.english: Three Versions of the Origin Legend & Genealogy of Apōdtho and Ramogi (Hobley 1903, pp. 326–331)
entries.translation: Apōdtho (descended on Ramogi/Lamogi Hill with cattle, mtama, sem-sem, wimbi, fire, spear, shield, and the Were tree; turned into a rock when his shadow was speared) → Version I (Ugada Ndiek of Usakwa): Apōdtho → Ramogi (Uyoma, Semi, Alego, Gemi, Nyakach, Umia Madok, Owidi, Rachonyo [Kandaia, Kanyaluo, Kaduong, Kabondo], Chwanya [Kisumu, Kanyamwa, Karungu, Kadem, Kaboch, Kachieng]) & Anyango • Version II (Ugada of Korando): Apōdtho → Chindu → Ramogi (Chingiruea → Owidi → Kisumu → Menya → Dedi → Tipo [Nyuto, Umwa, Okech, Nyawegi] → Korando → Abiru → Rombo → Otiendi → Ugada; Atipu → Kogonya; Kaponja; Kalachonyo; Nyakal → Semi; Kasilual → Umia Madok; Uwilo → Uyoma; Kaduet; Gemi loka ['on the other side']; Kanyada; Kadem; Karungu; Nyamkago; Lango) • Version III (Gori Kogalo of Kanyamwa): Apōdtho → Rajoki & Jimbo → Uyua → Ramogi (Mbunga, Uyoma, Semi, Chwanya [Uchieng, Kanyuta, Kalachonyo, Kabondo, Kisumu, Abonyo, Anyango, Beo, Kadem, Owiti, Kaboch], Nyamkago, Ujoa [Gemi, Alego], Alangu, Kanu [Koloa, Kubura]) & Mugirango
entries.pronunciation: a-po-dtho / ra-mo-gi / chwa-nya / u-yo-ma / se-mi / a-le-go / ge-mi
entries.context: C. W. Hobley (1903) 'British East Africa: Anthropological Studies in Kavirondo and Nandi', JAI Vol. 33, pp. 326–331

entries.english: Supreme Sun/Sky Deity, Daylight Sky & Four-Quarters Propitiation Ritual (Hobley 1903, pp. 343–344, 358 & Northcote 1907, p. 65)
entries.translation: Chieng' (used indifferently for the Sun and the Deity, believed to return east overhead behind the heavens at night) • Polo (the daylight sky, regarded as distinct from the sun's light, p. 358) • Spirit propitiation (pp. 343–344): throwing small pieces of meat, squirting mouthfuls of beer, and tossing spoonfuls of mtama porridge to the four quarters of the compass at the hut door
entries.context: C. W. Hobley (1903) 'Anthropological Studies in Kavirondo and Nandi', pp. 343–344, 358 & G. A. S. Northcote (1907, p. 65)

entries.english: Tho-Luo 8 Noun Plural Classes, Inclusive/Exclusive 'All' (waduto vs. giduto) & Gendered Salutations (Hobley 1902, pp. 61, 76, 84–87)
entries.translation: Inclusive vs. Exclusive 'All' (p. 61): waduto ('all of us', speaker included) vs. giduto ('all', other people/things) • Gendered Salutations (p. 76): ukwe (used by men) vs. amosi (used by women) • 8 Plural Classes (p. 87): Cl. I -tot (sere → seretot 'arrow', le → letot 'animal/axe'), Cl. II -ngnen / -wen (winyo → winyongnen 'bird', tong → tongwen 'egg/spear'), Cl. III e- → gi- (enuwadu → ginuwadu 'companion/brother'), Cl. IV -l → -k (diel → diek 'goat'), Cl. V -iji (chong → chongiji 'knee', lak → lakiji 'tooth'), Cl. VI -a/-o → -i (wer → weri 'song', rombo → rombi 'sheep'), Cl. VII unchanged (lueta 'arm/hand'), Cl. VIII irregulars (awang → wanga 'eye', diang → dok 'cow', ot → udi 'house', hega → hegini 'year')
entries.pronunciation: wa-du-to / gi-du-to / u-kwe / a-mo-si / di-ang dok / ot u-di
entries.context: C. W. Hobley (1902) 'Eastern Uganda: An Ethnological Survey', Ch. VI, pp. 61, 76, 84–87

entries.english: Married Woman's Grass Tassel (Chieno) & the Three-Goat Fine, Warrior Regalia & Huge Painted Buffalo Shields (Northcote 1907, pp. 58–59)
entries.translation: chieno (married woman's small grass tassel worn behind from the waist, discarded upon a husband's death until remarriage; anyone who touches a married woman's tassel must pay a fine of 3 goats to her husband, pp. 58–59) • Warrior regalia (p. 59): ostrich-feather or monkey/goat-skin hat, white bead lines across forehead/nose/lip/chin, cowrie leather baldric, black feather boa or wildebeest-tail shoulder ornament, iron-wire broad-bean-pod knee and ankle bells, and shaved crown hair-tuft cut off and worn by the chief mourner at his funeral • Weapons: long-hafted short-bladed spear (tong'), Masai sword, and huge curved buffalo-hide shield (kuot, ~3 ft 6 in high × nearly 6 ft horizontally, painted red, white, and black)
entries.context: G. A. S. Northcote (1907) 'The Nilotic Kavirondo', JRAI Vol. 37, pp. 58–59

entries.english: Strict Clan Exogamy, First-Wife Chieftaincy Succession & Pre-/Post-1883 Cattle-Plague Bride-Wealth (Northcote 1907, pp. 61–62)
entries.translation: Strict clan exogamy (p. 61): marriage within the clan is forbidden; a son may inherit his father's widow if not a blood relation, and two sisters may marry one man • Inheritance law (p. 61): each wife's allocated cattle pass to her own sons (her eldest son taking the largest share), and chieftaincy descends to the eldest son of the first/chief wife (mikayi) even if a junior wife bore an older son (or to an adult half-brother/eldest uncle if the heir is an infant, as regency is unknown) • Marriage rites & dowry (pp. 61–62): preliminary feast with an offering set aside for the sun-god (meat, chicken, mtama, and beer), ceremonial abduction, the bride's rite of cooking the first dinner at the groom's village to signify consent, and bride-wealth of 20 cattle before the 1883 cattle plague vs. 7 cattle (handsome dowry) or 1 heifer and 1 bull (or 1 bull and 20 goats) in 1907
entries.context: G. A. S. Northcote (1907) 'The Nilotic Kavirondo', JRAI Vol. 37, pp. 61–62

entries.english: Circular Village Architecture, Separate Family Huts & Wickerwork Granaries (Northcote 1907, pp. 60–61)
entries.translation: dala / pacho (circular homestead fenced with euphorbia ojuok hedge, stone wall, mud wall, or wattling) • kul (central open cattle pen) • dero (wickerwork granaries raised 2 ft off the ground, ~5 ft high × 3 ft diameter, circling the cattle pen) • Separate huts (udi): one for the husband, one for each wife, one for unmarried sons (simba), and one for unmarried daughters living with an old woman/grandmother (siwindhe)
entries.context: G. A. S. Northcote (1907) 'The Nilotic Kavirondo', JRAI Vol. 37, pp. 60–61

entries.english: 11 Personal Amulets & Charms of Chief Ugada Thako of Kisumu, Chieno Fibre Tail & Succession Law (Hobley 1903, pp. 345–347, 350–351, 358–359)
entries.translation: Ugada's 11 charms (pp. 345–347): 1. naming iron arrow points, 2. 3-holed iron strip from grandmother Thako, 3. lake quartz crystal in leather cup, 4. father Otiendi's perforated yellow stone, 5. Nya-Luo yellow beads, 6. goat-horn for chest, 7. chicken beak, 8. marine shell helix from Chief Ogalo of Kanyamwa, 9. omeni (4 small sticks on left wrist cord), 10. heavy brass bracelet from Aiyimbo, 11. skin bag for rheumatism • chieno (married woman's 6–8 inch stiff fibre tail made from tuoro aloe, pp. 350–351) • Succession law (p. 359): eldest son of the first-married wife (mikayi), e.g., Umoli + 1st wife Agola → Odera Ulalo & Sejenyi before 2nd wife Kakwari's older son Agina
entries.context: C. W. Hobley (1903) 'Anthropological Studies in Kavirondo and Nandi', JAI Vol. 33, pp. 345–347, 350–351, 358–359

entries.english: Owiti / Awiti ('Thrown-Away' Child Redemption Rite), Twins (Apio & Adongo), Nya-Luo Beads & Kiviri Ordeals (Hobley 1902, pp. 26–35)
entries.translation: Owiti (m.) / Awiti (f.): 3rd child born after two infant deaths is placed on a road at dawn, picked up by a neighbour woman, redeemed with a goat, adorned with a right-ear brass ring, and named Owiti/Awiti ('thrown away', p. 28) • Twins: Apio (1st) & Adongo (2nd) (p. 28) • Musical instruments: Thūm (8-string lyre), Būl (drum), Odundu (sorghum-stalk reed harp) (p. 30) • Ancient Nya-Luo blue/green/yellow jasper beads washed out after rain near Maragolia Hills (pp. 31–32) • Jamkingo (night wizard), Kiviri boiling-flour ordeal & mimosa-stopped calabash ordeal, and Ochola battle seed-case charm (pp. 32–34)
entries.pronunciation: o-wi-ti / a-wi-ti / a-pi-o / a-don-go / thum / bul / o-dun-du / nya-lu-o / ki-vi-ri

entries.english: Sir Harry Johnston's (1902, Vol. II, pp. 779–795) Ethnography of the Ja-luo (Nyifwa): Aluru/Japalua Kinship, Mother-in-Law Goatskin Rule, Papyrus Seines & Peacemaking
entries.translation: Origin & kinship (pp. 779–780): closely allied to the Acholi, Lango, Aluru, and Japalua ('Shefalu' of Northern Unyoro), called 'Abanyoro' by their Bantu Kavirondo neighbours • Dress & etiquette (pp. 781–787): married father must never visit his mother-in-law without wearing his small piece of goatskin (even underneath European trousers, under penalty of a goat fine); married woman's rear string tail must be worn when serving food to her husband, and touching it requires a goat sacrifice; 15 brass melon-seed-shaped rings with blue beads pierced along the outer ear-rim and ancient rain-washed nyaluo jasper/chalcedony beads near the Maragolia Hills worth 1 cow per bead; Nilotic stork-like one-legged resting posture • Subsistence & fishing (pp. 787–790): driving fish into conical wickerwork traps (dema) using papyrus-stalk seines and ambatch-wood rafts (Figs. 434–436), night torchlight fish-spearing, and blacksmith caste (Yothetth / Uvino) • Marriage, religion, ordeals & peacemaking (pp. 790–795): bride-wealth up to 6 cows; worshipping Chieng (the Sun) by spitting east in the morning and west in the evening; jamkingo secret magic vs. three kiviri ordeals (boiling wimbi flour pot, mimosa-stopped perforated calabash on a flat stone, and swallowing dry flour); 'thrown-away' child redemption rite naming the child Owiti (m.) / Awiti (f.) with a right-ear brass ring; chief buried in a new hut on an ox-hide with a water-pot over the head and seeds of every grain except sweet potatoes; warrior who slays an enemy hangs a live fowl by its beak around his neck and severs the body before entering the village; inter-tribal peace ratified by exchanging pieces of sheep flesh from a wooden grain-mortar and having an elder of the vanquished side sweep the conqueror's cattle kraal (p. 794)
entries.pronunciation: ja-lu-o / nyi-fwa / de-ma / yo-thetth / chieng / ki-vi-ri / o-wi-ti
entries.context: Sir Harry H. Johnston (1902) 'The Uganda Protectorate, Vol. II', Ch. XVIII, pp. 779–795

entries.english: Kadimu Python Ancestor Cult, Simbi Abūr Crater Legend & Bridge Island (Wa-Nyama kwa Wa-Ware) (Hobley 1903, pp. 326, 341–342, 349–350)
entries.translation: Kadimu (Bantu-origin clan speaking Dholuo at the Nzoia mouth who revere the python as their sacred common ancestor with annual hill sacrifices, pp. 326, 349) • Simbi abūr (abūr = 'hole or pit', natron crater lake in Kalachonyo formed when an inhospitable village was submerged by rain after a woman with fire-sparking eyes warned the one couple who fed her, pp. 349–350) • Wa-Nyama kwa Wa-Ware (Bridge Island near Lusinga/Rusinga, where two fighting bulls of the Wa-Nyama and Wa-Ware clans turned into twin granite monoliths, p. 341–342)

entries.english: Funeral Bull-Charging Dance, Recumbent In-Hut Burial (Correcting Eliot), Rain-Maker's Reed Ritual & 8-Stringed Harp (Northcote 1907, pp. 63–66)
entries.translation: Funeral rites (p. 63): doctors rattle stones in gourds and puff tobacco smoke to drive away evil spirits; warriors in war-paint charge with bulls while holding their tails; mother or chief wife wears the deceased's goatskin and hair-tuft while rattling a gourd; mock combat behind huge shields against invisible spirits; mourning lasts 6 days for a chief and 3 days for a commoner (wailing at sunrise and sunset); deceased body buried in a recumbent position inside his own hut (which continues to be occupied by his heir, correcting Sir Charles Eliot's claim that the hut is abandoned) • Rain-maker's ritual (p. 64): boils herbs in a large pot beneath a sacred big tree, transfers decoction to a small pot, blows through a hollow reed to make it bubble, and squirts the liquid into the air with incantations • Fishing & music (pp. 65–66): rod-and-line, sunken trawl lines, weirs, woven-grass nets, 4-pronged wooden fish-spears, hunting with dogs and throwing-sticks, and the 8-stringed harp (thum / nyatiti) accompanying extempore heroic and comic songs

entries.english: 13 Nilotic Kavirondo (Ja-Luo / Nife) Tribal Groups & 1900 Chiefs Recorded by C. W. Hobley (1902, pp. 52–56)
entries.translation: Ja-Luo (called Awa-Nife/Nyife or Awa-Nyoro by Bantu; clan prefixes Ja-, Ka-, Yaka-; language prefix Tho-): (1) Kami / Gemi (12 sub-tribes, chief Odera Ulalo), (2) Lego (7 sub-tribes, chief Ngongu), (3) Nife / Nyife (5 sub-tribes, chief Gero), (4) Kisumu (7 sub-tribes, chiefdi/Ugada), (5) Semi (6 sub-tribes), (6) Sembo (6 sub-tribes, chiefAmimo), (7) Uyoma (5 sub-tribes, chief Ndeda), (8) Sawakwa / Sakwa (6 sub-tribes, chiefUgada Thako), (9) Timu / Utimu [Kadimu] (5 sub-tribes, chief Anam), (10) Songa (chief Ugada), (11) Kanu / Kadibo [Wa-Kitoto] (12 sub-tribes, chief Kitoto), (12) Khoro, Kaki, Aiendi & Ramba (chief Ugwea), (13) Nyakatch & Kalachonyo (South Kavirondo, chief Gor)
entries.pronunciation: ja-lu-o / tho-lu-o / ge-mi / u-yo-ma / ka-di-mu / ka-nu
entries.context: C. W. Hobley (1902) 'Eastern Uganda: An Ethnological Survey', Ch. V, § 2, pp. 52–56

entries.english: Nilotic Origin, Dinka/Alur/Acholi Kinship near Wadilai & Secession Law (Northcote 1907, pp. 58–60)
entries.translation: Jaluo ('Nilotic Kavirondo'): belong to the same Nilotic family as the Dinka of the Sudan and are closely akin to the Aluri (Alur) and Acholi on both sides of the Nile near Wadilai; originally formed one tribe with the Acholi before migrating from the north-west under one big chief • Semi-feudal chieftaincies (Ruodhi) with sub-chiefs/headmen and an informal council of village heads (patres familiarum), where secession is the traditional constitutional check against an unpopular chief
entries.context: G. A. S. Northcote (1907) 'The Nilotic Kavirondo', JRAI Vol. 37, pp. 58–60
